strengths: High conceptual and practical importance: t-SNE is one of the most ubiquitous visualization tools in machine learning, biology, and other scientific fields; uncovering and formalizing its fundamental theoretical failure modes is of great value to the community.

Rigorous and elegant theoretical results: the paper provides clean mathematical proofs showing that (1) datasets with vanishingly weak cluster separation can have identical t-SNE stationary points as well-separated datasets, (2) near-simplex configurations can generate arbitrary stationary t-SNE outputs, and (3) stationary embeddings cannot depict extreme outliers beyond a constant bound (Theorem 9).

Compelling empirical demonstrations: the theoretical phenomena are convincingly illustrated on both synthetic configurations and real-world datasets (PBMC single-cell RNA-seq, credit card fraud detection, and BBC news text embeddings).

Clear, intuitive exposition and well-designed figures: the paper connects mathematical properties (e.g., additive distance shift invariance, affinity normalization asymmetry) to intuitive geometric visual failure modes such as cluster salience exaggeration and poison point vulnerability.
weaknesses: The core insight that adding a constant to squared pairwise distances leaves t-SNE affinities invariant has been noted previously in the literature (e.g., Lee & Verleysen, 2011, 2014), though the authors do cite these works and develop the implications on cluster indices and simplex geometry.

The formal proof of the poison point attack (Theorem 7) requires perplexity $\rho = 1$, which is an extreme regime not typically used by practitioners ($ho \approx 30\text{--}50$). While empirical experiments indicate degradation persists at higher perplexities, the mathematical guarantee does not cover typical perplexity values.

The analysis primarily focuses on stationary points of the objective function. In practice, t-SNE relies heavily on early exaggeration and specific initialization heuristics; further discussion on how initialization schemes interact with these stationary states would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Addresses an important and pervasive problem: while prior theoretical work on t-SNE focused almost exclusively on true positives (preserving well-separated clusters), this paper provides the first formal investigation into false positives, cluster exaggeration, and outlier misrepresentation.

The theoretical contributions are elegant and rigorous: Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 establish that identical clustered visualizations can originate from datasets with arbitrarily weak cluster separation; Theorem 5 and Lemma 6 characterize the extreme sensitivity around near-simplex data; and Theorem 9 provides a universal constant bound (roughly 3.266) on the depiction of outliers at stationarity.

The paper explains the core mathematical mechanisms driving these behaviors clearly, particularly the additive shift invariance of squared Euclidean distances in the Gaussian affinity formulation and the normalization asymmetry between input and output affinity distributions.

The practical implications are compelling and validated across synthetic and real-world datasets (e.g., PBMC3k single-cell transcriptomics, BBC news text embeddings, and credit card fraud detection), showing how adding even a single central point or adjusting distance scales can drastically alter or obscure structure.

The manuscript is well-written, clearly organized, contextualizes its findings honestly with prior literature (e.g., acknowledging Lee & Verleysen's observation of shift invariance), and provides complete proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core additive shift invariance property underlying Theorems 3 and 5 is an inherent consequence of softmax/normalized exponential kernels and has been observed previously in the literature (e.g., Lee & Verleysen, 2011), which slightly moderates the novelty of that specific observation, though formalizing its consequences on silhouette and cluster indices is novel.

Theorem 7 regarding the exact equivalence under single-point poison attacks is proved for perplexity rho = 1, which is an extreme parameter regime rarely used in practice (typical perplexity is 30–50). Although the empirical demonstrations show that vulnerability persists at larger perplexities, extending the formal proof to general perplexity regimes would strengthen the result.
The paper is primarily diagnostic and critical, focusing on uncovering fundamental failure modes without proposing algorithmic remediations or modified kernels to mitigate these issues.

strengths: Fundamental and timely topic: Despite t-SNE being one of the most widely used dimension reduction techniques in data science and bioinformatics, existing theory has mostly focused on guarantees for well-separated clusters. This work provides the first rigorous theoretical study of key failure modes: cluster salience exaggeration, extreme sensitivity to adversarial points, and outlier suppression.

Elegant and rigorous theoretical results: The paper delivers several surprising and clean theorems. Notably, Theorem 9 establishes a universal, input-agnostic upper bound on the outlier number (alpha <= 3.266 + o(1)) for any stationary t-SNE output, proving that t-SNE mathematically cannot depict extreme outliers. Lemma 6 and Theorem 3 convincingly establish that the entire image of t-SNE can be generated by inputs arbitrarily close to an unclustered regular simplex.

Insightful connection to high-dimensional geometry: The poison point analysis (Theorem 7 and Section 4.2.2) provides deep intuition into how high-dimensional distance concentration interacts with t-SNE's asymmetric affinity normalization, showing how a single centrally located point can completely collapse cluster structure.

Clear writing and compelling empirical validation: The theoretical findings are beautifully complemented by intuitive toy examples (simplex perturbations, Gaussian mixtures) and realistic experiments on standard datasets (PBMC3k scRNA-seq, BBC news embeddings, credit card fraud detection).
weaknesses: Prior work on additive invariance: The shift invariance of pairwise squared distances in SNE-like objectives was previously noted by Lee & Verleysen (2011, 2014). While the authors explicitly credit them and significantly extend the consequences to cluster validity indices and loss landscape equivalence, the fundamental invariance property itself is not entirely new.

Restriction of Theorem 7 to perplexity rho = 1: The theoretical proof for the poison point collapse is derived strictly in the limiting regime of rho = 1, where conditional distributions collapse to the nearest neighbor. Although empirical demonstrations in Figures 4, 6, and 10 confirm that this sensitivity persists under standard practical perplexities (e.g., rho in [30, 50]), extending the analytical guarantee to general rho remains an open question.

Interaction with standard optimization pipelines in practice: In practical workflows, t-SNE is rarely applied directly to raw high-dimensional coordinates without PCA preprocessing or early exaggeration. Although the authors provide an empirical ablation of PCA preprocessing in Appendix A.1 showing that distortions persist, a more prominent discussion in the main text on how early exaggeration and initialization interact with these failure modes would strengthen the work.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental and practically crucial question in data visualization: while previous work proved that well-clustered inputs produce well-clustered t-SNE embeddings, this work establishes the converse failure mode—namely, that strongly clustered visualizations can arise from arbitrarily unclustered inputs.

The theoretical insights are elegant, surprising, and sound. In particular, identifying the additive invariance of t-SNE with respect to squared pairwise distances (Lemma 16) provides a clear mathematical explanation for why high-dimensional datasets subject to measure concentration are easily distorted.

Theorem 8 provides a clean, input-agnostic upper bound on the outlier parameter (alpha <= 3 + o(1)) for stationary t-SNE embeddings, mathematically formalizing the empirical observation that t-SNE routinely absorbs extreme outliers into the main data mass.

The paper is very well-written, clearly organized, and balances mathematical rigor with intuitive explanations and practical demonstrations on synthetic, single-cell genomics, fraud detection, and text embedding datasets.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are framed in terms of stationary points (Definition 1). While Corollary 4 discusses global minimizers, standard practical implementations rely on specific optimization heuristics (e.g., early exaggeration and PCA initialization) that might affect which stationary points are reached in practice.

The construction of impostor datasets via Schoenberg's embedding theorem requires the ambient dimension to be n - 1. In many practical settings, n >> D, meaning the exact additive shift construction may not be embeddable in the original low-to-moderate ambient dimension without distortion.

While the paper demonstrates vulnerability to single-point 'poison' attacks, it would be beneficial to provide a more systematic quantification of how robust standard practitioner workflows (e.g., perplexity tuning, alternate initializations) are against such perturbations.

strengths: The paper provides an elegant and mathematically rigorous explanation for a widely observed practical problem: t-SNE's tendency to exaggerate or fabricate cluster structure.

The insight regarding the additive invariance of the input affinity matrix P with respect to squared pairwise distances—coupled with Schoenberg's theorem on Euclidean distance matrices—is simple, surprising, and theoretically profound.

Theorem 8 provides a clean, input-agnostic upper bound demonstrating that stationary t-SNE embeddings cannot portray extreme outliers (showing the outlier index is bounded by roughly 3), theoretically confirming why t-SNE often masks isolated points.

The paper is very well written and structured, complementing theoretical results with clear, illustrative figures and experiments on real-world datasets (e.g., PBMC3k single-cell RNA-seq, financial fraud detection, and BBC news embeddings).
The work has broad significance across machine learning, computational biology, and exploratory data analysis where t-SNE is heavily relied upon for scientific discovery and hypothesis generation.
weaknesses: The theoretical construction of the impostor datasets via classical MDS (Algorithm 1) generally embeds into ambient dimension D = n - 1; while high-dimensional datasets naturally exhibit measure concentration, a discussion on the minimum embedding dimension required for such impostor constructions would strengthen the practical framing.

The theorems characterize the set of stationary points and global minima of the t-SNE loss function rather than the algorithmic trajectory of gradient descent with early exaggeration, although empirical experiments appropriately bridge this gap.

The paper focuses solely on t-SNE; while briefly mentioning UMAP and TriMap in the discussion/related work, it would be beneficial to discuss whether similar additive invariance or outlier suppression holds for other popular neighbor-embedding techniques (e.g., UMAP, LargeVis).

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental, practically important, and understudied question in data visualization: the propensity of t-SNE to produce false positives (exaggerating cluster structure and suppressing outliers).

The theoretical insights are exceptionally clean, elegant, and mathematically rigorous. In particular, the identification of t-SNE's invariance to additive shifts in squared pairwise distances (and its realization via Schoenberg's embedding theorem) provides an illuminating explanation for why arbitrarily unclustered datasets can yield identical t-SNE embeddings to clustered ones.

Theorem 8 establishes an impressive, input-agnostic upper bound (alpha <= 3 + o(1)) on how far an outlier can be depicted in the embedding space due to the asymmetric normalization in t-SNE's probability formulation. This formally explains the well-known empirical phenomenon of outliers being collapsed into the bulk.

The theoretical results are well-supported by intuitive synthetic experiments and compelling real-world case studies (e.g., single-cell PBMC3k, financial fraud detection, and BBC news text embeddings).
The manuscript is clearly written, well-organized, and contextualizes its findings appropriately within the existing literature on t-SNE guarantees and empirical criticisms.
weaknesses: To embed the additively shifted distance matrix X_{+C} into Euclidean space via Schoenberg's theorem (Lemma 15), the dimension typically needs to be D = n - 1. While this is relevant for modern high-dimensional settings (genomics, text embeddings), it would strengthen the paper to discuss the limitations of this construction when D << n.

The theoretical treatment of outliers in Section 5 and Theorem 8 is restricted to a single outlier (x_0). While the paper mentions that this can be generalized and tests multi-outlier cases empirically, providing formal bounds for multiple outliers would broaden the theoretical contribution.
